findings.title: The linking -en- rule also removes final stress from Latinate -endeer/-enseer verbs.
findings.body:
The new rules apply to any vowel, consonant, `en`, an L20 onset, then a final `ee`. L20 leaves out `t`, but it includes `d` and `s`. So Latinate verb forms such as `agendeer`/`agendeert`, `amendeer`/`amendeert`, `recenseer`/`recenseert` and `gecondenseerd` now match `@CenL20) ee (r_`, `(rt_` or `(rd_`. They get unstressed `I` in place of the stressed `'I`, and these words lose their only correct stress.

None of these is a linking -en- compound. Fix: narrow the context, for example by also leaving `d` and `s` out of the onsets used for the `ee (r…` variants, or add the affected stems as exceptions.

findings.title: `model` has no guard for `modellen`/`modelleren`, unlike `hotel`, `tabel` and `snel`.
findings.body:
The siblings `snel`, `hotel` and `tabel` each get a `(le` rule so that inflections with a doubled `l` are not split as compounds. `model` only gets `(C@P5` and `(l@P5`, so `modellen`, `modelleren` and `modellering` match `model (l@P5`.

What goes wrong: `model` is split off as a stressed prefix `mo:d'E`, and the rest (`len`, `leren`) is translated as a second word. `modelleren` then gets primary stress on `-del-` instead of on `-le-`. `modellen` most likely gets a wrong final syllable too, the same failure the `snel (le` guard and the `sneller` test were added to prevent.

Fix: add `_) model (le  mo:d'El` before the `l@P5` rule, as for `hotel` and `tabel`.
findings.suggestion:
_) model (le      mo:d'El        // not a compound (nl-compound-stress exc)
           _) model (l@P5    mo:d'E         // compound, final consonant not doubled (nl-compound-stress exc)

findings.title: Common adjectives derived from compounds now get first-element stress (oorspronkelijk, huishoudelijk).
findings.body:
Adjectives in `-elijk` and `-ig` built on compounds take stress on the second element, which is why the PR adds `hoofdzakelijk`, `levensgevaarlijk` and `kunstmatig` to `nl_list`. Several equally common words of this kind are not covered, and the new prefix rules now catch them:
- `oorspronkelijk` and `oorzakelijk` match `oor (C@P3`
- `huishoudelijk` matches `huis (C@P4`
- `spreekwoordelijk` matches `spreek (C@P6`

Each comes out stressed on the first syllable (`'O:r...`, `h'Wys...`, `spr'e:k...`) instead of oorspr'onkelijk, huish'oudelijk and spreekw'oordelijk.

Fix: add these words to the exception block in `nl_list`, or add `(spronk` / `(houd` style guards without `P`, like the existing `-ig` manual rules.
